findings.title: On date-override days the busy-time check is skipped entirely, allowing double bookings
findings.body: In checkIfIsAvailable, when a date override exists for the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the code reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` (line 133) and returns 'available' before ever evaluating the `busy.every(...)` check at line 153. Since this function is now used to validate every candidate slot against each fixed host of a round-robin event (and against loose hosts), any existing booking or calendar busy time a host has on a date-override day is ignored and the slot is offered anyway, so the host can be double-booked. A matching date override should only bypass the working-hours check; the busy/busy-calendar check must still run.

findings.title: Working-hours guard computes the slot end from the slot start time
findings.body: In the new working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is an exact copy of the `start` computation — it never adds eventLength, so the upper-bound comparison `end > workingHour.endTime` only checks the slot's start. A slot that starts inside a fixed host's working hours but ends after them (e.g. a 60-minute event starting 15 minutes before the host's day ends) passes the guard and is shown as bookable, booking the host outside their availability. `end` should be derived from the slot end time (slot start + eventLength).

findings.title: Fixed host with no working hours at all on the slot's weekday is treated as available
findings.body: The new working-hours guard only rejects a slot when it finds a workingHour entry whose `days` includes the slot's weekday AND the slot is outside that entry's window. If the fixed host has no availability row for that weekday (e.g. they don't work weekends), `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined, the guard passes, and only busy times are checked. For a round-robin event, slots generated from another (non-fixed) host's schedule on the fixed host's day off are therefore still offered — exactly the kind of over-booking this PR is meant to prevent. A weekday with no matching working-hours entry should be treated as unavailable.

findings.title: Slots inside one of several same-day override windows are rejected
findings.body: The `dateOverrides.find(...)` at line 106 returns truthy as soon as ANY override on the slot's date does not contain the slot (slot ends at/before that override's start, or starts after its end). When a host has multiple override windows on the same day (e.g. 09:00–11:00 and 14:00–16:00), a slot at 10:00 is inside the first window but 'outside' the second, so find() returns the second override and the function returns false — the slot is hidden even though the host is available. The slot should be considered covered if it fits inside ANY of that day's override windows. Additionally the boundary is off by one: `slotStartTime.isAfter(overrideEnd)` is strict, so a slot starting exactly at an override's end is treated as inside the override and returned as available although it lies outside every window.

findings.title: `===` between two Dayjs objects is always false, making the blocked-day branch dead code
findings.body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares two freshly created Dayjs instances by object identity, so it can never be true. The intent was evidently `.isSame()` to detect zero-length overrides (start == end, i.e. a fully blocked day). As written, blocked-day detection falls through to the other conditions, which happen to reject most slots but let a slot starting exactly at the override start pass, and the dead branch misleads anyone maintaining this logic.

findings.title: The fixed-host date-override fix for round-robin events has no automated test
findings.body: The PR's headline change — applying fixed hosts' date overrides and working hours in checkIfIsAvailable for round-robin events (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts) — is only covered by manual testing steps. The single added test exercises a personal event's slot generation with a different invitee timezone. The new checkIfIsAvailable logic has several interacting branches (override match, blocked day, working-hours bounds, busy times) and contains regressions a test would catch, e.g. a fixed host with a date override plus a conflicting existing booking is currently shown as available. A round-robin scenario with a fixed host who has a date override and a busy period on that day should be added.

findings.title: Offset conversion of overrides discards day overflow when the shift crosses midnight
findings.body: The invitee-local override start/end are computed as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + .minute()`. If applying `offset` (invitee offset minus organizer offset) pushes the time across midnight — e.g. an 00:30–02:00 override for an Asia/Kolkata host viewed by a UTC-4 invitee becomes 09:30 the previous day — `.hour()/.minute()` keep only the time-of-day and the day shift is lost. Combined with the `activeOverrides` filter, which matches overrides by the organizer-local date against the invitee's day, such overrides produce slots at the wrong time on the wrong day instead of on the adjacent invitee day.

findings.title: Override date matching formats in server-local timezone against a UTC slot time
findings.body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` creates the Dayjs in the server's local timezone (no `.utc()`), while the slot side `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')` is in UTC mode. The two date strings can therefore disagree for the same instant on any host not running in UTC, causing overrides to fail to match (or match the wrong day) depending on deployment timezone. Relatedly, when `organizerTimeZone` is undefined the offset silently falls back to 0, treating the override's wall-clock times as UTC.

findings.title: Override conversion relies on optional timeZone with no fallback
findings.body: `TimeRange.timeZone` was added as optional, but the conversion does `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` unconditionally and never falls back to the `organizerTimeZone` parameter that getSlots already receives. Any caller passing dateOverrides without a timeZone gets the server's own offset as 'organizer offset', silently converting override times as if they were UTC. The `override.start.toString()` round-trip also makes dayjs parse a non-ISO locale string instead of just passing the Date object, which is fragile and triggers dayjs's non-ISO parse warning.
